config.title: German Courses in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: What a Berlin German course costs per teaching unit, which routes can be free, and what changes the moment you pass B1.

items.q: How much does a German course cost in Berlin?
items.a: It depends on your level far more than on the school. Up to and including B1, Berlin law caps a Volkshochschule German course at 130 per cent of the federal integration-course contribution. That contribution is 2.29 euro per teaching unit, so the ceiling is about 2.98 euro for 45 minutes and the floor is 80 cents. A hundred teaching units therefore costs between 80 and 298 euro. Above B1 the cap stops and the normal Volkshochschule band applies, between half and two and a half times the 3.20 euro base value, so 1.60 to 8.00 euro a unit. Private schools in Berlin publish anything from about 5.45 euro a unit for a monthly intensive course up to 10 euro a unit at the weekly rate, before registration and materials.

items.q: Why did Berlin course prices go up this summer?
items.a: The Senate ordinance that governs Volkshochschule fees sets a Basiswert, a base value per 45-minute teaching unit, and every course is priced between 50 and 250 per cent of it. That base value was 2.76 euro from August 2023 and rose to 3.20 euro on 1 August 2026, an increase of about 16 per cent. It moves whenever the teaching fee rates move, by the same percentage on the same date. It does not change the German-course ceiling below B1, because that ceiling is tied to the federal integration-course figure instead.

items.q: Does my student card or Berlin-Ticket S make a German course cheaper?
items.a: Only above B1, and this catches people out constantly. The Berlin ordinance says the individual 50 per cent reductions do not apply to German courses that fall under the capped rule, and that rule covers everything up to and including B1. From B2 upwards the normal fee band applies and the reduction comes back. The half-price list is long: Berlin-Ticket S holders, people on Sozialhilfe, Buergergeld, Wohngeld, Kinderzuschlag, Arbeitslosengeld, Kurzarbeitergeld or Asylbewerberleistungen and their household, full-time students at state or state-recognised universities, apprentices, school leavers without a place for up to twelve months, people doing Bundesfreiwilligendienst or a voluntary year, and holders of the Ehrenamtskarte Berlin-Brandenburg.

items.q: Can I learn German in Berlin for free?
items.a: Yes, on three routes. Some Volkshochschule courses carry no fee at all: literacy courses and parent courses should be free, and courses advertised for people whose first language is not German can be free, at the head of school’s discretion. The Integrationskurs contribution can be waived entirely if you are on Buergergeld, Sozialhilfe or a low salary, but you must apply before the course starts because it is only backdated to your first module. And the Berufssprachkurs above B1 is free unless you are employed with taxable income over 20,000 euro a year. All three need paperwork rather than money, which is why so many people who qualify never use them.

items.q: What is the Integrationskurs and what does it really cost?
items.a: It is the federal course: 600 teaching units of language taking you to B1, plus a 100-unit orientation course on law, history and society, ending with the Leben in Deutschland test. At 2.29 euro a unit the full 700 units comes to 1,603 euro, and you pay it in blocks of 100 units, not in one payment. Two things reduce that. You can be exempted from the contribution on benefits or a low income, and if you pass the final test within two years of the entitlement being issued you can get half your contribution back, which brings 1,603 euro down to roughly 800.

items.q: What is a Berufssprachkurs and am I eligible?
items.a: It is the job-related German course under the federal DeuFoeV regulation, and it starts where the Integrationskurs stops. The standard blocks are 400 teaching units from B1 to B2 and another 400 from B2 to C1, with a longer course of usually 500 units for C2. Participation is free in principle. You pay only if you are in employment subject to social insurance and your taxable income is over 20,000 euro a year, or 40,000 for a jointly assessed couple, and then it is 2.56 euro a unit, so 1,024 euro for a 400-unit course. Half comes back when you pass, and your employer is allowed to pay your share. You need a Berechtigungsschein first, usually through the Agentur fuer Arbeit, the Jobcenter or the local Volkshochschule advice counter.

items.q: Can I book a Volkshochschule German course online?
items.a: No. Unlike a pottery or yoga course, registration for German and integration courses at the Berlin Volkshochschulen happens in person, after a placement test and an advice appointment, and you need your passport or identity card with you. Volkshochschule Mitte, for example, runs its German counter at Antonstrasse 37 in Wedding on Mondays and Thursdays from 11:00 to 14:00 and Tuesdays from 14:00 to 17:00. You can book the appointment online and walk-ins are accepted. The autumn and winter semester starts in September, and the programme is published four to six weeks beforehand, so the good intensive slots go early.

items.q: Is Bildungszeit worth using for a German course in Berlin?
items.a: It is the most under-used thing in this article. Berlin’s Bildungszeitgesetz gives an employee on a five-day week five working days of paid leave per calendar year for a recognised course, and you may pull the following year’s entitlement forward to take ten days in one block if your employer agrees. You qualify six months into the job. Two rules decide whether it helps you: unused days cannot be carried into the next calendar year, so the entitlement expires on 31 December, and recognition is granted course by course, so the listing either carries the Bildungszeit label or it does not. Ten consecutive weekday mornings of intensive German paid by your employer beats six months of evening classes you keep missing.

items.q: What happens if I book a course and then cannot go?
items.a: The Berlin Volkshochschule cancellation rule is stricter than most people expect. You can cancel free of charge within 14 days of booking. After that a cancellation fee of 20 per cent of the fee applies, with a minimum of 10 euro, and fees of 10 euro or less are not refunded at all. From the fifth day before the course begins you cannot cancel at all and the full fee is due. Free courses carry no cancellation fee. The practical consequence is simple: book the course you will actually attend, not the ambitious one, because the deadline arrives about a week before you have started.

items.q: How many Volkshochschulen are there in Berlin and does it matter which one I use?
items.a: Twelve, one per district: Charlottenburg-Wilmersdorf, Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg, Lichtenberg, Marzahn-Hellersdorf, Mitte, Neukoelln, Pankow, Reinickendorf, Spandau, Steglitz-Zehlendorf, Tempelhof-Schoeneberg and Treptow-Koepenick. They all price under the same Senate ordinance, so the fee rules are identical wherever you go. What differs is the timetable, the building, the counter hours and which levels each one is running this term. You are not tied to the Volkshochschule of the district you live in, so if your local counter has nothing at your level, ask the next one along before you reach for a private school.
